prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN)  -- Colombian officials are blaming the FARC guerrilla group for a car bombing late Sunday at a police station in Cali that killed two people and wounded at least 14. Residents check out a destroyed police building after a car bombing Sunday night in Cali, Colombia. It was the second bombing in Colombia attributed to the Marxist guerrilla group in less than a week. An explosion at a Blockbuster video rental store in an upscale Bogota neighborhood Tuesday killed two and wounded more than 20. The suspect in Sunday night's attack was killed in a shootout with police after the explosion, Cali Mayor Jorge Ivan Ospina said Monday, hours after convening a special security meeting in the middle of the night. "Although the explosive device only had moderate impact," Ospina said on the Cali government Web site, "we should not forget we are at war and the FARC has been committing terrorist acts in Bogota, Neiva, Cali and other cities in the country. That's why we cannot let our guard down, since they take advantage of Sundays and city centers, where control is more difficult." The explosion came just hours after the rebel group released four hostages in what many interpreted as a gesture to reach a peace accord with the government. Two officials also are slated to be released this week. FARC, which is the Spanish acronym for Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, is the largest and oldest revolutionary group in the nation and has been at war with the government for more than 40 years. According to Ospina, a blue and red Renault 12 Break pickup crashed into the police headquarters in Cali at 10:38 p.m. and then exploded. The driver tried to flee but was felled by two shots from uniformed police and died a few hours later at a hospital, the mayor said. The explosion caused damage in a two-block area, the Cali news Web site Semana.com said. Five of the 14 wounded were minors, Ospina said, citing emergency director Laureano Quintero. The injured are suffering from fractures and other wounds not considered life-threatening, he said. Cali's health minister, Alejandro Varela, said earlier 32 were wounded, including a pregnant woman who was in good condition. Others complained of hearing problems. The mayor's office said the previous higher tally could be a result of people not wounded in the bombing but seeking medical attention to receive government help. Three police were wounded, including a major with a broken arm and an officer who had to have three fingers amputated on his left hand, said the police chief, Gustavo Adolfo Ricaurte Tapia. The bombing caused a temporary power outage, which made security more difficult for officials, said the news Web site Burladero.com. It was the fourth bombing in Cali in less than 42 months, Semana.com said. The latest bombing took place about five blocks from the Palace of Justice, which was blasted by a car bomb in August, killing four and wounding 26. Police buildings were bombed in April 2007 and August 2006. The earlier blast killed five and wounded 17, Semana.com said. Security analysts say FARC has about 9,000 to 12,000 armed guerillas and several thousand supporters, mostly in rural areas. The guerrilla group was established in 1964 as the military wing of the Colombian Communist Party. The guerrillas operate mostly in Colombia but have carried out extortion, kidnappings and other activities in Venezuela, Panama and Ecuador, according to the Federation of American Scientists Intelligence Resource Program. Authorities said Sunday night's bomb contained 90 kilograms (198 pounds) of ammonium nitrate fertilizer and fuel, a commonly used explosive, Semana.com said. By comparison, the bomb that Timothy McVeigh used in the 1995 bombing in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, contained more than 2,800 kilos (6,200 pounds) of ammonium nitrate and diesel fuel.

FARC, the Spanish acronym for the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, is the country’s largest and oldest revolutionary group and has been at war with the government for more than 40 years.

According to Ospina, a blue and red Renault 12 Break pickup crashed into the police headquarters in Cali at 10:38 p.m. and then exploded. The driver attempted to flee but was struck by two shots fired by uniformed police officers and died several hours later at a hospital, the mayor said.

The latest attack occurred about five blocks from the Palace of Justice, which was struck by a car bomb in August, killing four people and wounding 26. Police buildings were also bombed in April 2007 and August 2006. The earlier blast killed five people and wounded 17, Semana.com said.

Security analysts estimate that FARC has about 9,000 to 12,000 armed guerrillas and several thousand supporters, most of them in rural areas. The guerrilla group was founded in 1964 as the military wing of the Colombian Communist Party.

The guerrillas operate primarily in Colombia but have carried out extortion, kidnappings and other activities in Venezuela, Panama and Ecuador, according to the Federation of American Scientists Intelligence Resource Program.

People in the area surveyed the wreckage of the police facility after the Sunday night blast in Cali. It was the second attack in Colombia in under a week that officials linked to the Marxist rebel group. The previous Tuesday, a bomb at a Blockbuster video rental shop in an affluent district of Bogota killed two people and injured more than 20.

Cali Mayor Jorge Ivan Ospina said Monday that the person suspected of carrying out Sunday night’s bombing died after exchanging gunfire with police following the explosion. Ospina spoke hours after calling an emergency security meeting in the middle of the night.

“Although the explosive device only had moderate impact,” Ospina said in a statement posted on the Cali government website, “we should not forget we are at war and the FARC has been committing terrorist acts in Bogota, Neiva, Cali and other cities in the country. That's why we cannot let our guard down, since they take advantage of Sundays and city centers, where control is more difficult.”

The attack occurred only hours after the rebel movement freed four hostages, a move widely viewed as a possible signal of interest in negotiating peace with the government. Two public officials were also expected to be released later in the week.

FARC, short for the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia in Spanish, is Colombia’s oldest and largest rebel organization and has fought the government for more than four decades.

According to Ospina, a blue-and-red Renault 12 Break pickup truck rammed into the police headquarters in Cali at 10:38 p.m. and then detonated. The mayor said the driver attempted to escape but was struck by two shots fired by uniformed officers and died several hours later in a hospital.

The blast damaged an area covering roughly two blocks, the Cali news site Semana.com reported.

Ospina, citing emergency director Laureano Quintero, said five of the 14 injured people were children or teenagers. He said the victims had fractures and other injuries that were not believed to be life-threatening.

Earlier, Cali Health Minister Alejandro Varela had reported 32 injuries, including a pregnant woman who was said to be in good condition. Other people reported problems with their hearing.

The mayor’s office said the earlier, larger injury count may have included people who were not actually hurt in the bombing but sought medical care in hopes of qualifying for government assistance.

Police chief Gustavo Adolfo Ricaurte Tapia said three police officers were injured. Among them were a major who suffered a broken arm and an officer whose left hand required the amputation of three fingers.

The explosion also briefly knocked out electrical service, making security efforts more difficult for authorities, the news website Burladero.com reported.

Semana.com said the incident was the fourth bombing in Cali in less than 42 months. The latest attack happened about five blocks from the Palace of Justice, where a car bomb exploded in August, killing four people and wounding 26. Police facilities were also attacked with bombs in April 2007 and August 2006. The earlier of those explosions killed five people and injured 17, according to Semana.com.

Security experts estimate that FARC has between 9,000 and 12,000 armed fighters, along with several thousand supporters, most of them based in rural regions.

The group was formed in 1964 as the armed branch of the Colombian Communist Party. Although its operations are centered mainly in Colombia, the Federation of American Scientists Intelligence Resource Program says the guerrillas have also engaged in extortion, kidnappings and other activities in Venezuela, Panama and Ecuador.

Authorities said the device used in Sunday night’s bombing contained 90 kilograms, or 198 pounds, of ammonium nitrate fertilizer mixed with fuel, a commonly used explosive combination, Semana.com reported.

For comparison, the bomb used by Timothy McVeigh in the 1995 attack in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, contained more than 2,800 kilograms, or 6,200 pounds, of ammonium nitrate and diesel fuel.

**CALI, Colombia —** A car bomb exploded late Sunday outside a police station in Cali, Colombia, killing and injuring civilians and police officers in an attack authorities blamed on the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC.

The blast struck near the station in the city’s urban center, damaging nearby buildings, shattering windows and sending residents into the streets, officials said. Authorities reported multiple casualties, including police personnel and civilians, though officials said the toll could change as emergency crews continued assessing the scene.

“This was a terrorist act directed against the police and the civilian population,” a senior Colombian security official said, blaming FARC guerrillas for the bombing. “The state will respond with all of its capacity.”

Police said investigators were searching for a suspect believed to have driven or parked the explosives-laden vehicle near the station shortly before the detonation. Officials described the suspect as a man who abandoned the vehicle and fled the area moments before the blast. Security cameras and witness statements were being reviewed, police said.

Cali, one of Colombia’s largest cities and a major commercial hub in the southwest, has faced periodic attacks linked by authorities to guerrilla and criminal groups operating in the surrounding Valle del Cauca and Cauca regions.

The bombing followed other attacks Colombian officials have attributed to FARC, including car bombings and explosives attacks targeting police stations, government buildings and military patrols. Authorities have said the group has used such attacks to retaliate against security operations and to demonstrate its ability to strike in urban areas.

FARC, founded in the 1960s as a Marxist guerrilla movement, fought the Colombian state for decades and funded itself through kidnapping, extortion and the drug trade, according to Colombian and U.S. officials. At its height, the group controlled large rural areas and carried out bombings, ambushes and kidnappings across the country.

Colombian authorities have long designated FARC as a terrorist organization. The United States and European Union also listed the group as a terrorist organization during the conflict. A peace agreement signed in 2016 led to the demobilization of the main FARC organization, though dissident factions rejected the accord and continue to operate in parts of Colombia.

Officials said security had been increased around police installations in Cali as forensic teams examined the blast site and investigators worked to identify those responsible.

Colombia’s government blamed the attack on a faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, that rejected a 2016 peace agreement and continues to operate as an armed dissident group. Officials said the bombing bore the hallmarks of recent attacks attributed to rebels seeking to pressure security forces and intimidate civilians in areas where armed groups compete for control of drug trafficking routes.

The blast comes amid a deteriorating security situation in parts of southwestern Colombia, where FARC dissident factions, the National Liberation Army guerrilla group and criminal organizations have expanded their presence in rural corridors used for cocaine production and transport.

Although the main FARC rebel movement signed a peace deal with the Colombian government in 2016 and disarmed, several splinter groups refused to demobilize or later returned to arms. The government refers to them as FARC dissidents and has accused them of kidnappings, extortion, attacks on security forces and bombings in recent years.

**Car Bombing Rocks Cali, Colombia, as Mayor Blames FARC Amid Tensions Over Hostage Releases**

*CALI, Colombia —* A powerful car bomb exploded in the southwestern Colombian city of Cali, injuring dozens of people and causing extensive damage to government buildings, businesses and nearby homes, in an attack authorities linked to the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC.

The blast occurred in a busy area of the city, shattering windows across several blocks, damaging storefronts and vehicles, and leaving streets littered with glass, twisted metal and debris. Emergency crews rushed the wounded to hospitals as police and military units cordoned off the area and searched for additional explosives.

Officials reported that **at least two dozen people were injured**, with some suffering wounds from flying glass and debris. Local authorities said the number could rise as hospitals continued to evaluate victims. Damage assessments found severe impact to nearby offices and commercial buildings, with windows blown out and facades cracked by the force of the explosion.

Cali Mayor **Jorge Iván Ospina** condemned the bombing, calling it an attack on civilians and on the city’s stability. He said authorities believed the bombing bore the hallmarks of FARC tactics and urged residents to remain calm while security forces investigated.

“This is a cowardly act of terrorism,” Ospina said in comments to local media. “Cali will not be intimidated. We will respond with unity, with institutional strength and with support for the victims.”

The bombing came at a sensitive moment in Colombia’s long-running internal conflict, following renewed attention on **FARC hostages**. In recent years, the guerrilla group had released several captives, including politicians, police officers and soldiers held for years in jungle camps. Those releases were often framed by FARC as humanitarian gestures, but Colombian officials and victims’ families continued to denounce the group’s kidnapping campaign as one of the most painful legacies of the conflict.

The most dramatic hostage development came in 2008, when Colombian security forces rescued former presidential candidate **Íngrid Betancourt**, three U.S. defense contractors and 11 Colombian police and military personnel in **Operation Jaque**, a bloodless intelligence operation that dealt a major blow to FARC’s leadership and morale. Other hostages had been freed earlier through negotiated releases, often involving international mediators.

Authorities said the Cali bombing appeared intended to show that FARC retained the ability to strike urban targets despite military setbacks and leadership losses. Security analysts noted that the group had increasingly used explosives, car bombs and attacks on infrastructure as its conventional battlefield capacity weakened under government offensives.

Founded in 1964, **FARC** began as a Marxist guerrilla movement claiming to represent poor farmers and rural communities against Colombia’s political and economic elite. Over decades, it grew into Latin America’s largest insurgent group, financing itself through kidnapping, extortion, illegal mining and the cocaine trade, according to Colombian and U.S. officials. At its height, FARC controlled or influenced large rural zones and carried out attacks on military, police, political and economic targets.

But by the late 2000s, the organization was under heavy pressure. Colombian military operations had killed or captured key commanders, disrupted supply routes and reduced the group’s territorial control. The government of then-President Álvaro Uribe pursued a hardline security strategy aimed at weakening FARC militarily while demanding the unconditional release of hostages.

In Cali, residents described scenes of panic after the explosion. Witnesses said the blast sounded like “a thunderclap” and was followed by screams, car alarms and smoke rising from the street. Shopkeepers swept glass from entrances as rescue workers helped injured pedestrians away from the area.

Municipal officials said engineers would inspect affected buildings to determine whether any structures were unsafe. Police also appealed to the public for information about suspicious vehicles or people seen near the blast site before the explosion.

Mayor Ospina said the city would increase security around public buildings, transportation corridors and commercial zones, but he insisted that normal life in Cali should continue.

“The answer to terror is solidarity,” he said. “We stand with the injured, with their families and with all citizens who refuse to surrender their city to violence.”

counterfactuals.output:
# Colombia on alert after FARC-dissident bombings, with Cali police station attack intensifying security fears

**CALI, Colombia —** Colombian authorities are on heightened alert after a new wave of bombings attributed to FARC dissident factions, including an attack targeting a police station in Cali that has sharpened fears of an expanding urban campaign by armed groups operating in the country’s southwest.

Officials said the Cali attack appeared to fit a pattern of recent assaults against police posts, military patrols, municipal buildings and civilian areas in Valle del Cauca and neighboring Cauca — departments that have become central battlegrounds between the Colombian state and breakaway guerrilla factions that rejected or abandoned the 2016 peace accord with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, known as the FARC.

The explosion near the Cali police facility sent shockwaves through surrounding neighborhoods, damaging nearby buildings and vehicles and prompting a rapid deployment of police, army units and emergency responders. Authorities attributed the attack to FARC dissident structures active in the region, though investigations were ongoing and officials cautioned that forensic teams were still analyzing the type of explosive device used and whether the bomb was detonated remotely.

Casualty figures remained subject to official updates, but emergency personnel reported injuries among security forces and civilians in the area. Local authorities said residents were treated for blast-related wounds, shock and injuries from shattered glass and debris. The attack also forced temporary road closures and security cordons around the station as bomb disposal units searched for secondary devices.

“This was an attack not only against the police but against the population,” a local security official said, describing the blast as part of a wider effort by armed groups to intimidate communities and weaken state presence.

## A troubling shift toward urban targets

The Cali police station bombing has raised particular concern because Cali, Colombia’s third-largest city and the economic hub of the southwest, has long been a strategic prize for armed groups seeking access to transportation routes, ports, illicit markets and political visibility. While rural zones of Cauca, Nariño and Valle del Cauca have endured years of conflict involving guerrillas, criminal groups and narcotics networks, attacks inside or near major urban centers carry a different psychological and political impact.

Security analysts say FARC dissident factions have increasingly used explosive attacks to demonstrate operational reach, retaliate against police and military pressure, and disrupt government efforts to expand control in contested areas.

The latest bombing follows previous attacks in the southwest, including car bombs, motorcycle bombs, explosive devices planted near police stations, and ambushes against security patrols. In several cases, authorities have blamed dissident units associated with the former FARC’s regional fronts, particularly groups operating under structures such as the Estado Mayor Central or affiliated local fronts. These factions are not part of the demobilized FARC political movement that emerged from the 2016 peace deal.

## Previous attacks and mounting casualties

Colombia’s southwestern corridor has seen repeated violence in recent months and years. Police stations and municipal buildings in towns across Cauca and Valle del Cauca have been targeted with explosives, often leaving civilians among the wounded. Attacks in places such as Jamundí, Morales, Suárez, Corinto and other municipalities have underscored the vulnerability of both urban outskirts and rural town centers.

In prior incidents attributed to FARC dissidents, explosives have been placed in vehicles or motorcycles and detonated near police installations. Such attacks have killed or wounded police officers, soldiers and civilians, and have caused extensive property damage. Authorities have also reported attacks on roads, bridges, electrical infrastructure and government buildings — tactics designed to stretch security forces and generate public fear.

The toll has added pressure on President Gustavo Petro’s administration, which has pursued a policy of “total peace” aimed at negotiating with multiple armed groups. While the government has opened channels with some organizations, ceasefires have repeatedly frayed amid accusations of kidnappings, extortion, recruitment of minors, attacks on security forces and continued involvement in drug trafficking.

The southwest remains especially volatile because of its geography and illicit economy. Mountain corridors, jungle routes and proximity to the Pacific coast make the region valuable for cocaine production and trafficking. Armed factions also fight for control over illegal mining, extortion networks and strategic transit routes.

## Security response in Cali and Valle del Cauca

Following the Cali attack, police increased patrols around stations, transport terminals, public buildings and major roads. Authorities also urged residents to report suspicious packages, abandoned vehicles or unusual activity near security installations.

The army has been expected to reinforce operations in areas surrounding Cali and nearby municipalities where dissident fighters are believed to move between rural strongholds and urban support networks. Intelligence units are investigating whether the bombing involved local collaborators, logistical cells or explosives transported from rural zones.

Security officials said preventing additional attacks will require not only heavier patrols but improved intelligence coordination between police, military and prosecutors. Colombian authorities have often warned that dissident groups rely on small urban cells to conduct surveillance, move explosives and identify targets.

Residents of Cali expressed fear and frustration after the blast, with some calling for stronger protection of neighborhoods surrounding police facilities. In Colombia, police stations are frequent targets in conflict zones, but they are often located in densely populated areas, increasing the risk to civilians when bombings occur.

## FARC’s origins and the rise of dissident factions

The FARC was founded in 1964 as a Marxist-Leninist guerrilla movement rooted in rural peasant self-defense groups. For decades, it waged war against the Colombian state, claiming to fight for land reform and social justice while financing itself through kidnapping, extortion, illegal mining and, increasingly, the cocaine trade.

At its peak, the FARC had thousands of fighters and controlled or influenced large swaths of rural Colombia. The conflict among guerrillas, paramilitary groups, drug traffickers and state forces left hundreds of thousands dead and millions displaced.

A landmark peace agreement signed in 2016 between the Colombian government and the FARC led to the disarmament of the main guerrilla organization and its transformation into a legal political party. But not all commanders and fighters accepted the deal. Some refused to demobilize from the outset, while others later returned to arms, citing security failures, slow implementation of rural reforms, internal divisions or opportunities in criminal economies.

These splinter groups are commonly known as FARC dissidents. They vary in size, ideology and command structure. Some retain political language from the old insurgency, while others operate more like criminal organizations focused on drug trafficking and territorial control. Colombian officials generally distinguish between the demobilized FARC political party and dissident armed groups that continue to conduct attacks.

## A test for Petro’s peace policy

The bombing in Cali poses a significant test for the Petro government, which has argued that Colombia cannot end its cycles of violence through military force alone. Critics, however, say armed groups have used negotiations and ceasefires to expand, rearm and consolidate territory.

Government officials have defended dialogue efforts while promising firm action against groups that attack civilians and security forces. In practice, the state faces a difficult balance: pursuing talks where possible while responding militarily to factions accused of bombings, kidnapping and drug trafficking.

For many Colombians, the latest attack revived memories of earlier eras of urban terrorism and guerrilla violence. Though Colombia’s security situation has changed dramatically since the height of the conflict, the persistence of armed groups in rural regions — and their ability to strike cities — remains a major national concern.

As investigators examine the Cali bombing, authorities are warning that further attacks cannot be ruled out. Police have urged calm but remain on alert, especially in the southwest, where the struggle between the state and FARC dissidents appears far from over.

“This is a developing situation,” officials said, noting that casualty numbers, responsibility claims and operational details may change as the investigation advances.
